title: Rebase vs Merge
description: Compare rebase and merge strategies, understand their trade-offs, and know when to use each.

data.text: Rebase and merge are the two primary strategies for integrating branches. They produce different history shapes, have different conflict behaviors, and signal different things about your team's workflow. Understanding both deeply — and when to use each — is a hallmark of a senior Git user.

data.title: Visual comparison
items: **Merge**: Produces a merge commit with two parents. History shows exactly when branches were integrated.
**Rebase + merge**: Replays commits linearly onto the target, then fast-forward merges. History is clean and linear.
**Squash merge**: Combines all feature branch commits into one. History is clean but loses granularity.
Keeping a feature branch up to date with main during development
Preparing a PR for review with a clean, linear history
Integrating frequent small changes with minimal merge noise
Teams that have adopted trunk-based development
Integrating a finished feature or release branch into main
Preserving the true integration timeline for audit or release notes
Teams that want to see exactly when branches were merged
Public/shared branches that cannot be rewritten

data.title: Rebase then fast-forward merge (recommended for feature branches)
data.code:
# On your feature branch — rebase onto main
git rebase origin/main

# On main — fast-forward merge
git switch main
git merge --ff-only feature/auth

# Result: linear history, no merge commit

data.title: Regular merge (preserves integration history)
data.code:
# On main — merge the feature branch
git switch main
git merge feature/auth --no-ff

# Result: merge commit showing the integration point

data.title: The hybrid approach
data.text: Rebase feature branches during development, then merge them into main with --no-ff. This gives you clean development history and clear integration points.

rows: Rewrites history — unsafe on shared branches

items: GitHub: Settings > General > Merge button > Allow merge commits / Squash and merge / Rebase and merge
GitLab: Settings > General > Merge requests > Merge method
Bitbucket: Repository settings > Workflow > Merge strategy > Rebase

items.question: Is rebase always better than merge?
items.answer: No. Rebase is better for local branch updates. Merge is better for integrating public branches and preserving integration history. Both have valid use cases.

items.question: Can I merge without a merge commit?
items.answer: Yes. If the branch you are merging is an ancestor of the current branch, Git performs a fast-forward merge by default. Use --no-ff to always create a merge commit.

items.question: What is the --ff-only flag?
items.answer: git merge --ff-only merges only if a fast-forward is possible. If not, it fails instead of creating a merge commit.

items.question: Does rebase break pull requests?
items.answer: Only if you rebase a branch that is already the source of an open PR. Most platforms handle force-pushed branches correctly. Always use --force-with-lease to be safe.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Rebase for clean, linear history — merge for preserving integration points
Rebase conflicts are sequential; merge conflicts are resolved once
Use --force-with-lease after rebasing a remote branch
Never rebase commits that are already on a shared/public branch
The hybrid approach: rebase during development, merge for integration
